title: Merge Sort: A Divide-and-Conquer Algorithm
text:
Algorithms can be designed using various fundamental approaches. Two primary techniques are:

Incremental Approach: Used by algorithms like Insertion Sort. It builds the solution one element at a time (e.g., inserting a single element into an already sorted subarray).
Divide-and-Conquer Approach: A highly recursive alternative that often yields significantly faster worst-case running times. It solves problems by breaking them down into smaller, manageable pieces.

title: Merge Sort: A Divide-and-Conquer Algorithm
text:
Algorithms can be designed using various fundamental approaches. Two primary techniques are:

Incremental Approach: Used by algorithms like Insertion Sort. It builds the solution one element at a time (e.g., inserting a single element into an already sorted subarray).
Divide-and-Conquer Approach: A highly recursive alternative that often yields significantly faster worst-case running times. It solves problems by breaking them down into smaller, manageable pieces.

title: Merge Sort: A Divide-and-Conquer Algorithm
text:
2. The Divide-and-Conquer Paradigm
This recursive approach involves three distinct steps at each level of the recursion:

Divide: Break the original problem into a number of smaller subproblems that are just smaller instances of the exact same problem.
Conquer: Solve the subproblems recursively. However, if the subproblem size is small enough (the recursion “bottoms out”), solve it in a straightforward, direct manner.
Combine: Merge the solutions of the smaller subproblems together to formulate the solution to the original, overarching problem.

title: Merge Sort: A Divide-and-Conquer Algorithm
text:
3. Merge Sort Overview
Merge Sort is a classic algorithm that strictly follows the divide-and-conquer paradigm to sort a sequence of elements:

Divide: Split the sequence into two separate subsequences of equal (or near-equal) size.
Conquer: Recursively sort both subsequences using Merge Sort. This process bottoms out when a sequence hits a length of 1, as a single element is already inherently sorted.
Combine: Merge the two sorted subsequences back together to produce the final, fully sorted answer.

The Brief Idea: The algorithm works by recursively tracing the array indices all the way down to the base cases (single elements) first, and only then performs the merging process on the way back up the call stack.

title: Merge Sort: A Divide-and-Conquer Algorithm
text:
4. The MERGE-SORT Pseudocode
To sort an array, we need a function that drives the divide-and-conquer process.



Line
MERGE-SORT(A, p, r)




1
if \(p < r\)


2
    \(q = \lfloor(p + r)/2\rfloor\)


3
    MERGE-SORT(A, p, q)


4
    MERGE-SORT(A, q + 1, r)


5
    MERGE(A, p, q, r)



To sort an entire sequence \(A = \langle A[1], A[2], \dots, A[n] \rangle\), we make the initial call MERGE-SORT(A, 1, A.length). The algorithm consists of repeatedly merging pairs of smaller sorted sequences to form larger ones until the final sorted sequence is formulated.

## 6. The MERGE Procedure
The crucial operation in Merge Sort is the “combine” step, handled by an auxiliary procedure called MERGE(A, p, q, r).

Function: It assumes that the two subarrays \(A[p \dots q]\) and \(A[q+1 \dots r]\) are already sorted. It merges them into a single sorted subarray that replaces \(A[p \dots r]\).
Card Analogy: Imagine two sorted piles of cards face up on a table. You compare the top two cards, remove the smaller one, and place it face down in a new output pile. You repeat this constant-time comparison step until all cards are merged.
Time Complexity: Because each basic step compares two cards and takes constant time, merging \(n\) total elements takes \(\Theta(n)\) time.
Sentinels: To prevent the algorithm from constantly needing to check if either pile is completely empty, a special “sentinel” card containing the value infinity (\(\infty\)) is placed at the bottom of each pile. This guarantees that the core sorting logic stops exactly when all real data has been merged.

title: Merge Sort: A Divide-and-Conquer Algorithm
text:
7. MERGE Pseudocode
Below is the pseudocode for the merging process, demonstrating the use of the new temporary arrays (\(L\) and \(R\)) and the sentinel values.







Line
MERGE(A, p, q, r)




1
\(n_1 = q - p + 1\)


2
\(n_2 = r - q\)


3
let \(L[1 \dots n_1 + 1]\) and \(R[1 \dots n_2 + 1]\) be new arrays


4
for \(i = 1\) to \(n_1\)


5
    \(L[i] = A[p + i - 1]\)


6
for \(j = 1\) to \(n_2\)


7
    \(R[j] = A[q + j]\)


8
\(L[n_1 + 1] = \infty\)     // Sentinel value


9
\(R[n_2 + 1] = \infty\)     // Sentinel value


10
\(i = 1\)


11
\(j = 1\)


12
for \(k = p\) to \(r\)


13
    if \(L[i] \le R[j]\)


14

15
        \(i = i + 1\)


16
    else \(A[k] = R[j]\)


17
        \(j = j + 1\)




Understanding the MERGE(A, p, q, r) Procedure
To understand exactly how this pseudocode works, let’s trace it using a concrete example.

Our Setup
Imagine we have an array \(A\) (using 1-based indexing, as the textbook does):
\[
A = [8, 4, 7, 2, 5, 9]
\]
We want to merge two sorted sections in the middle of this array:

The left sorted pile: \([4, 7]\) (located at indices 2 and 3)
The right sorted pile: \([2, 5]\) (located at indices 4 and 5)

We call MERGE(A, 2, 3, 5). Here, \(p = 2\) (start), \(q = 3\) (middle), and \(r = 5\) (end).



Part 1: Figuring Out the Sizes

Line 1: \(n_1 = q - p + 1\)

Math: \(n_1 = 3 - 2 + 1 = 2\)
Meaning: We calculate the number of elements in the left pile. The left pile has 2 elements (\([4, 7]\)).

Line 2: \(n_2 = r - q\)

Math: \(n_2 = 5 - 3 = 2\)
Meaning: We calculate the number of elements in the right pile. The right pile has 2 elements (\([2, 5]\)).





Part 2: Creating the Left and Right Piles

Line 3: let L[1 .. n_1 + 1] and R[1 .. n_2 + 1] be new arrays

Meaning: We create two empty temporary arrays, \(L\) (Left) and \(R\) (Right). We make them one slot bigger than \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) (size 3) to make room for the special “sentinel” card at the bottom.

Lines 4–5: for \(i = 1\) to \(n_1 \implies L[i] = A[p + i - 1]\)

Meaning: Copy the left sorted section from array \(A\) into our new array \(L\).
When \(i = 1\): \(L[1] = A[2 + 1 - 1] = A[2] = 4\)
When \(i = 2\): \(L[2] = A[2 + 2 - 1] = A[3] = 7\)
Result: \(L = [4, 7, ?]\)

Lines 6–7: for \(j = 1\) to \(n_2 \implies R[j] = A[q + j]\)

Meaning: Copy the right sorted section from array \(A\) into our new array \(R\).
When \(j = 1\): \(R[1] = A[3 + 1] = A[4] = 2\)
When \(j = 2\): \(R[2] = A[3 + 2] = A[5] = 5\)
Result: \(R = [2, 5, ?]\)

Lines 8–9: \(L[n_1 + 1] = \infty\) and \(R[n_2 + 1] = \infty\)

Meaning: Place the sentinel value (infinity) at the end of both temporary arrays. This acts as a wall so we never run out of bounds during comparison.
Result: \(L = [4, 7, \infty]\) and \(R = [2, 5, \infty]\)





Part 3: The Merging Process

Lines 10–11: \(i = 1\) and \(j = 1\)

Meaning: We set our “pointers”. \(i\) points to the top card of the Left pile (\(L[1] = 4\)). \(j\) points to the top card of the Right pile (\(R[1] = 2\)).

Lines 12–17: for \(k = p\) to \(r\)

Meaning: This is the main loop. We will look at the slots in the original array \(A\) from index \(p = 2\) to \(r = 5\), and figure out which number goes there by comparing the tops of piles \(L\) and \(R\).



Loop Iterations

Loop Iteration 1 (\(k = 2\)):

Compare (Line 13): Is \(L[1]\) (which is \(4\)) \(\le R[1]\) (which is \(2\))? No.
Action (Lines 16–17): The right card is smaller. Put \(R[1]\) into the main array at \(A[2]\). Move the right pointer down (\(j = 2\)).
Array \(A\) is now: \([8, 2, 7, 2, 5, 9]\)

Loop Iteration 2 (\(k = 3\)):

Compare (Line 13): Is \(L[1]\) (which is \(4\)) \(\le R[2]\) (which is \(5\))? Yes.
Action (Lines 14–15): The left card is smaller. Put \(L[1]\) into the main array at \(A[3]\). Move the left pointer down (\(i = 2\)).
Array \(A\) is now: \([8, 2, 4, 2, 5, 9]\)

Loop Iteration 3 (\(k = 4\)):

Compare (Line 13): Is \(L[2]\) (which is \(7\)) \(\le R[2]\) (which is \(5\))? No.
Action (Lines 16–17): The right card is smaller. Put \(R[2]\) into the main array at \(A[4]\). Move the right pointer down (\(j = 3\)).
Array \(A\) is now: \([8, 2, 4, 5, 5, 9]\)

Loop Iteration 4 (\(k = 5\)):

Compare (Line 13): Is \(L[2]\) (which is \(7\)) \(\le R[3]\) (which is \(\infty\))? Yes. (This is why the sentinel is genius! Any real number is less than \(\infty\), so it forces the remaining cards in \(L\) to be picked up).
Action (Lines 14–15): The left card is smaller. Put \(L[2]\) into the main array at \(A[5]\). Move the left pointer down (\(i = 3\)).
Array \(A\) is now: \([8, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9]\)





Conclusion
The loop finishes because \(k\) reached \(r = 5\).
Our original array \(A\) went from \([8, 4, 7, 2, 5, 9]\) to \([8, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9]\).
The target section from indices 2 through 5 is now perfectly merged and sorted!

title: Merge Sort: A Divide-and-Conquer Algorithm
text:
8. Concrete Example: Tracing Merge Sort
To understand how Merge Sort operates in practice, let us trace the algorithm on an unsorted 8-element array:
\[
A = [5, 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 2, 6]
\]

Step 1: The Divide Phase
The algorithm recursively splits the array in half until every subsequence contains only a single element:

Split 1: \([5, 2, 4, 7]\) and \([1, 3, 2, 6]\)
Split 2: \([5, 2]\), \([4, 7]\), \([1, 3]\), and \([2, 6]\)
Base Case (Length 1): \([5]\), \([2]\), \([4]\), \([7]\), \([1]\), \([3]\), \([2]\), and \([6]\)

At this point, the recursion bottoms out because sequences of length 1 are trivially sorted.


Step 2: The Combine Phase (Merging)
The auxiliary procedure MERGE combines the small sorted subarrays back together level-by-level:

Merge to size 2: \([2, 5]\), \([4, 7]\), \([1, 3]\), and \([2, 6]\)
Merge to size 4: \([2, 4, 5, 7]\) and \([1, 2, 3, 6]\)
Final Merge to size 8: We call MERGE on the two halves \(L = [2, 4, 5, 7]\) and \(R = [1, 2, 3, 6]\).

title: Insertion Sort Algorithm
text: An insertion sort works exactly like sorting a hand of playing cards: you pick up cards one by one from an unsorted pile and slide each new card into its correct position among the cards you are already holding.

title: Insertion Sort Algorithm
text: An insertion sort works exactly like sorting a hand of playing cards: you pick up cards one by one from an unsorted pile and slide each new card into its correct position among the cards you are already holding.

title: Insertion Sort Algorithm
text:
Visualizing the Partition
To see this in action, let’s sort five numbers from smallest to largest: [5, 3, 8, 4, 2].
Imagine dividing the list into two sections separated by a vertical bar: a sorted section on the left, and an unsorted section on the right.

title: Insertion Sort Algorithm
text:
The Step-by-Step Trace

Starting Position: [5 | 3, 8, 4, 2]
We start by looking at the very first number, 5. Since it is the only number in our “sorted hand,” it is already sorted by default.


Step 1: Pick up 3
We look at the first unsorted number (3) and compare it to the sorted section on the left. Since 3 is smaller than 5, we shift 5 one spot to the right and drop 3 into the empty space at the front.
Current state: [3, 5 | 8, 4, 2]


Step 2: Pick up 8
We take the next unsorted number (8) and compare it moving from right to left in our sorted section. Is 8 smaller than 5? No. Since it is already larger than the biggest number in our hand, we don’t need to shift anything — it simply locks into place on the end.
Current state: [3, 5, 8 | 4, 2]


Step 3: Pick up 4
We take 4 and compare it moving leftwards:
Smaller than 8? Yes — shift 8 to the right. Smaller than 5? Yes — shift 5 to the right. Smaller than 3? No! We stop here and insert 4 into the spot right between 3 and 5. Current state: [3, 4, 5, 8 | 2]


Step 4: Pick up 2
Finally, we take 2 and compare it against our sorted hand. Since 2 is smaller than 8, 5, 4, and 3, all four of those numbers shift one position to the right, opening up the very first spot for 2.
Final sorted list: [2, 3, 4, 5, 8]

\(c_i\) represents the constant time cost to execute line \(i\) exactly once.
Different operations (math, assignments, conditional checks) require slightly different processing times, hence unique costs (\(c_1, c_2, \dots\)).

For an input array of size \(n\):

Outer loop body (Lines 2, 4, 8): Runs \(n - 1\) times (one less than the header).
Inner while loop condition (Line 5): Runs \(\sum_{j=2}^n t_j\) times, where \(t_j\) is the number of condition checks during the \(j\)-th pass.

\[
T(n) = c_1n + c_2(n-1) + c_4(n-1) + c_5 \sum_{j=2}^n t_j + c_6 \sum_{j=2}^n (t_j - 1) + c_7 \sum_{j=2}^n (t_j - 1) + c_8(n-1)
\]

title: Theoretical Analysis of Insertion Sort
text:
2. Concrete Example Trace: \(A = [3, 1, 2]\)
Let us trace the algorithm using an input size of \(n=3\) and hypothetical execution cycles for each \(c_i\).

Step A: Setting up Constants
Assume the following clock cycle costs per execution:

\(c_1 = 2\) cycles (checking for loop, incrementing \(j\))
\(c_2 = 1\) cycle (reading and assigning key)
\(c_4 = 1\) cycle (assigning \(i\))
\(c_5 = 3\) cycles (checking while conditions)
\(c_6 = 2\) cycles (shifting element right)
\(c_7 = 1\) cycle (decrementing \(i\))
\(c_8 = 1\) cycle (inserting key)



Step B: Tracing the Loops to Find \(t_j\)

Pass \(j = 2\) (Inserting 1 into \([3]\)): The condition is checked once successfully, and once failing (\(3>1\), then \(0>0\) fails). Result: \(t_2 = 2\) (loop body runs \(1\) time).
Pass \(j = 3\) (Inserting 2 into \([1, 3]\)): The condition is checked once successfully, and once failing (\(3>2\), then \(1>2\) fails). Result: \(t_3 = 2\) (loop body runs \(1\) time).



Step C: Computing Total Time \(T(3)\)
Substituting \(n=3, t_2=2, t_3=2\) into our frequencies:

Line 1: \(n = 3\) times
Lines 2, 4, 8: \(n-1 = 2\) times each
Line 5: \(t_2 + t_3 = 4\) times
Lines 6, 7: \((t_2-1) + (t_3-1) = 2\) times each

Multiplying by the \(c_i\) costs and summing:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(3) &= (c_1 \times 3) + (c_2 \times 2) + (c_4 \times 2) + (c_5 \times 4) + (c_6 \times 2) + (c_7 \times 2) + (c_8 \times 2) \\
     &= (2 \times 3) + (1 \times 2) + (1 \times 2) + (3 \times 4) + (2 \times 2) + (1 \times 2) + (1 \times 2) \\
     &= 6 + 2 + 2 + 12 + 4 + 2 + 2 \\
     &= \mathbf{30 \text{ cycles}}
\end{aligned}
\]
Conclusion: For this unsorted array, it takes 30 cycles. If the array were already sorted (e.g., \([1, 2, 3]\)), the inner loop would fail immediately (\(t_2=1, t_3=1\)). This eliminates Lines 6 and 7, dropping the total running time to a much faster 18 cycles.

title: Theoretical Analysis of Insertion Sort
text:
3. Best-Case and Worst-Case Scenarios
Even for inputs of the exact same size \(n\), the algorithm’s running time can vary drastically depending on how the initial items are arranged.

The Best-Case: Already Sorted

Scenario: The input array is already in the correct sorted order.
What happens: When the inner while loop checks if it needs to shift elements, it immediately finds they are in order (\(A[i] \le key\)).
Math impact: The condition is checked exactly once per pass (\(t_j = 1\)). The inner loop body never runs (\(t_j - 1 = 0\)).
Calculation: Substituting \(t_j = 1\) into our \(T(n)\) formula gives:

\[
\begin{aligned}
T(n) &= c_1n + c_2(n-1) + c_4(n-1) + c_5(n-1) + c_8(n-1) \\
     &= (c_1 + c_2 + c_4 + c_5 + c_8)n - (c_2 + c_4 + c_5 + c_8)
\end{aligned}
\]

Resulting Time: We can express this running time as \(T(n) = \mathbf{an + b}\) (where \(a\) and \(b\) are constants), which is a fast, linear function of \(n\).



The Worst-Case: Reverse Sorted

Scenario: The input array is completely backward (decreasing order).
What happens: The inner while loop must shift every new element all the way to the very front, comparing it against every single item in the already-sorted portion.
Math impact: The loop condition is checked \(j\) times per pass (\(t_j = j\)).
Applying Summations: We replace the sums in our \(T(n)\) formula using standard math rules:

\[
\sum_{j=2}^n j = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} - 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{j=2}^n (j-1) = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}
\]

Calculation: Substituting these formulas into our \(T(n)\) equation gives:

\[
\begin{aligned}
T(n) &= c_1n + c_2(n-1) + c_4(n-1) + c_5\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{2} - 1\right) \\
     &\quad + c_6\left(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\right) + c_7\left(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\right) + c_8(n-1) \\
     &= \left(\frac{c_5}{2} + \frac{c_6}{2} + \frac{c_7}{2}\right)n^2 + \left(c_1 + c_2 + c_4 + \frac{c_5}{2} - \frac{c_6}{2} - \frac{c_7}{2} + c_8\right)n - (c_2 + c_4 + c_5 + c_8)
\end{aligned}
\]

Resulting Time: We can express this worst-case time as \(T(n) = \mathbf{an^2 + bn + c}\) (where \(a, b,\) and \(c\) are constants), which is a significantly slower, quadratic function of \(n\).
